extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in geometric analysis / Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions and proofs around Perelman's reduced volume, the κ-noncollapsed condition, Perelman's no-local-collapsing theorems (I, I′, II), and Hamilton's compactness/convergence results for Ricci flow solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's reduced volume finiteness and monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: ˜V(τ) = (4π τ)^{-n/2} ∫_M e^{-l(q,τ)} dV_τ(q) is finite and nonincreasing in τ; the monotonicity is strict unless we are on a gradient shrinking soliton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses properties of L-geodesics, Jacobian estimates as τ → 0 (limits (3.2.18), (3.2.19)), Shi's derivative estimates, and Theorem 3.2.7 (Jacobian comparison) to show finiteness and then monotonicity. Equality (no strict monotonicity) characterizes gradient shrinking solitons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 3.3.1 — κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on scale r
rubrics_metrics.description: A Ricci flow solution g_ij(t) is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on scale r if whenever on the parabolic neighborhood (x,t) ∈ B_{t0}(x0,r) × [t0 - r^2, t0] one has |Rm(x,t)| ≤ r^{-2}, then Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bt0(x0,r) is the geodesic ball at time t0. This is the local volume noncollapse condition used throughout the no-local-collapsing results; κ and r are positive constants to be produced in theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.3.2 — No Local Collapsing Theorem I (Perelman)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any initial metric g_ij on a compact n-manifold M and the Ricci flow solution g_ij(t) on [0,T), there exist positive constants κ and ρ0 (depending on the initial data) such that for any t0 ∈ [0,T) and any x0 ∈ M the solution is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on all scales less than ρ0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using sequences of pointed rescalings, Perelman's reduced volume ˜V(τ) monotonicity, Jacobian and reduced-distance estimates, and Shi's estimates. The theorem gives a uniform local injectivity/volume lower bound in terms of local curvature bounds and survives surgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.3.3 — No Local Collapsing Theorem I′ (scalar-curvature variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is compact and g_ij(t), 0 ≤ t < T, is a solution of the Ricci flow, then there exists κ > 0 depending only on the initial metric and T such that whenever at time t0 we have R(x,t0) ≤ r^{-2} on Bt0(x0,r) with 0 < r ≤ √T, then Vol_{t0}(Bt0(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stronger version replaces the full curvature tensor bound by only a scalar curvature bound. Proof uses the µ-functional/W-functional: choose a cutoff test function f (with ζ), estimate W(g,f,τ) and use lower bounds on µ(g(0),·) to derive a lower volume bound; several quantitative constants (µ0, ζ choices) enter the estimate for κ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3.4.1 — Parabolic Laplacian comparison and distance-time derivative estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If Ric(·,t0) ≥ −(n−1)K on B_{t0}(x0,r0), then at t = t0 and outside B_{t0}(x0,r0) the distance function d(x,t)=d_t(x,x0) satisfies the differential inequality ∂_t d − Δ d ≥ −(n−1)( (2/3) K r0 + r0^{-1} ). (ii) If Ric(·,t0) ≥ −(n−1)K on both B_{t0}(x0,r0) and B_{t0}(x1,r0), then at t = t0 one has an estimate d/dt d_t(x0,x1) ≥ −(2/3)(n−1)(K r0 + r0^{-1}) (up to the constants stated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma is a parabolic analogue/generalization of Laplacian comparison without sign restriction, and generalizes Hamilton's result using second variation and index comparison-type arguments. The inequalities are used in maximum-principle arguments and in controlling the evolution of distance under Ricci flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.4.2 — No Local Collapsing Theorem II (Perelman)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any A>0 there exists κ(A)>0 such that: if g_ij(t) is a complete Ricci flow solution on [0,r0^2] with bounded curvature and satisfying |Rm|(x,t) ≤ r0^{-2} for (x,t) ∈ B_0(x0,r0)×[0,r0^2] and Vol_0(B_0(x0,r0)) ≥ A^{-1} r0^n, and if d_{r0^2}(x,x0) ≤ A r0, then g_ij(t) is κ-noncollapsed on all scales less than r0 at every point (x,r0^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses scaling (take r0=1), reduced volume ˜V(τ), the estimate of reduced-distance ¯L via a differential inequality (3.4.1) and a maximum-principle argument with cutoff φ(d(y,t)/A(2t + 1)) to control minima of a modified ¯L. The theorem gives a relative (local) noncollapsing estimate depending only on A and local initial volume and curvature bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition 4.1.1 — C^∞_loc convergence of marked geodesic balls / marked manifolds
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of marked geodesic balls (B(p_k, s_k), g_k, p_k) (0 < s_k ≤ s_∞) converges in the C^∞_loc topology to a marked (possibly noncomplete) ball (B(p_∞, s_∞), g_∞, p_∞) if there exist exhausting open sets U_k ⊂ B(p_∞, s_∞) and diffeomorphisms f_k: U_k → V_k ⊂ B(p_k, s_k) with f_k(p_∞)=p_k such that the pullback metrics (f_k)^* g_k converge to g_∞ in C^∞ on every compact subset of B(p_∞, s_∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion applies to sequences of (possibly noncompact) marked manifolds; it differs from convergence of metrics on a fixed manifold because the diffeomorphisms f_k may move points. It is the topology used in Hamilton's compactness theorem for Ricci flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 4.1.2 — Hamilton's compactness / convergence theorem (local version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let (M_k, g_k, p_k) be marked complete Riemannian n-manifolds and consider geodesic balls B(p_k,s_k) with s_k → s_∞ (0 < s_∞ ≤ +∞). Suppose (a) for every r < s_∞ and every integer ℓ there exist bounds B_{ℓ,r} with |∇^ℓ Rm(g_k)| ≤ B_{ℓ,r} on B(p_k,r); and (b) inj(M_k,p_k) ≥ δ > 0 uniformly. Then a subsequence of (B(p_k,s_k), g_k, p_k) converges in C^∞_loc to a marked geodesic ball (B(p_∞, s_∞), g_∞, p_∞). If s_∞ = +∞ the limit is complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem adapts Hamilton's result to allow noncompact limits, avoid global diameter or global injectivity radius hypotheses, and permit only local curvature bounds. Proof uses local injectivity radius estimates, selection of covering balls with uniform coordinate charts, diagonal subsequence arguments, and construction of approximate isometries between large finite-radius pieces.
